variants.title: Trace one global step
variants.context: One coherent global step assigns deterministic work to every rank, computes local tensors, exchanges the state the chosen layout requires, then applies a consistent optimizer update and commits recoverable progress.
variants.prompt: A synchronous job completes one optimizer step. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Exchange required state with the collectives the layout calls for, such as all-reduce, all-gather, or stage sends.
Update and commit progress by applying a consistent optimizer step, advancing the data position, and publishing a recoverable checkpoint.
Assign deterministic work by partitioning examples or tokens per data-parallel rank, including the uneven final batch.
Compute local tensors by running the local model partition to produce activations, losses, and gradients.

variants.hint: Which stage decides what each rank is even responsible for?
variants.explanation: Every rank must derive its update from the intended batch and synchronization contract, so ownership is settled before any tensor is computed.

variants.title: Trace one global step
variants.context: One coherent global step assigns deterministic work to every rank, computes local tensors, exchanges the state the chosen layout requires, then applies a consistent optimizer update and commits recoverable progress.
variants.prompt: A fully sharded job holds only parameter shards between steps. Put its step in order.

items.text: Forward and backward run locally and produce gradients for the reconstructed module.
A reduce-scatter reduces those gradients and leaves each rank holding only its own shard.
The optimizer updates the locally owned shard and the global step advances.
The ranks all-gather the parameter shards a module needs so it can be computed.
Each rank receives its assigned micro-batch from the sharded input pipeline.

variants.hint: Sharded training pays communication to avoid holding the whole model.
variants.explanation: Full sharding reconstructs parameters only for as long as a module needs them, which is why all-gather precedes compute and reduce-scatter follows it.

variants.title: Trace one global step
variants.context: One coherent global step assigns deterministic work to every rank, computes local tensors, exchanges the state the chosen layout requires, then applies a consistent optimizer update and commits recoverable progress.
variants.prompt: A pipeline-parallel job streams micro-batches across two stages that are also data-parallel replicas. Put the step in order.

items.text: The final stage computes the loss and starts the backward pass back through the stages.
The optimizer step is applied and the global step counter advances together on every rank.
The first stage computes its layers and sends activations to the next stage point to point.
Gradients are all-reduced across the data-parallel replicas of each stage.
Micro-batches are assigned to data-parallel ranks with an intentional owner for the uneven tail.

variants.hint: Tensor and pipeline ranks collaborate on the same examples rather than adding new ones.
variants.explanation: Pipeline stages exchange activations point to point while gradient synchronization stays inside each data-parallel group.

variants.title: Diagnose the scaling regression
variants.context: A scaling regression is diagnosed in order: measure one rank and the full group, look at the maximum rather than the mean, separate bandwidth limits from latency limits, inspect placement against the link hierarchy, then change one variable at a time against the same workload.
variants.prompt: Adding nodes stopped improving throughput. Put the diagnosis steps in order.

items.text: Separate bandwidth limits from latency limits by comparing few large collectives against many small ones.
Measure input, forward, backward, collective, and checkpoint time for one rank and for the full group.
Change one variable, such as bucket size, micro-batch count, or group layout, against the same measured workload.
Inspect placement so tensor-parallel and sharding groups sit on high-bandwidth links before crossing nodes.
Look for the maximum rather than the mean, because one slow rank sets a synchronous boundary.

variants.hint: Averages hide the rank that everyone else is waiting on.
variants.explanation: Synchronous workers meet at communication boundaries, so the slowest rank determines step time even when average utilization looks fine.

variants.title: Diagnose the scaling regression
variants.context: A scaling regression is diagnosed in order: measure one rank and the full group, look at the maximum rather than the mean, separate bandwidth limits from latency limits, inspect placement against the link hierarchy, then change one variable at a time against the same workload.
variants.prompt: Average GPU utilization reads 85 percent but step time is far above target. Put the investigation in order.

items.text: Check whether that rank is waiting on data decoding, a remote read, or an imbalanced shard.
Break the step into input, compute, collective, and checkpoint time per rank instead of trusting a cluster average.
Re-test after changing only the suspected variable so the effect can be attributed.
Rank the results by the slowest participant at each synchronization boundary.
Confirm whether its collectives are bandwidth bound on bytes or latency bound on many small launches.

variants.hint: A high average is compatible with one rank stalling every step.
variants.explanation: Stragglers hide behind cluster averages, so the distribution and the slowest rank are inspected at every synchronization boundary.

variants.title: Diagnose the scaling regression
variants.context: A scaling regression is diagnosed in order: measure one rank and the full group, look at the maximum rather than the mean, separate bandwidth limits from latency limits, inspect placement against the link hierarchy, then change one variable at a time against the same workload.
variants.prompt: A job slowed down right after the tensor-parallel degree was raised from 2 to 8. Put the checks in order.

items.text: Find the slowest rank in the enlarged tensor-parallel group rather than the group average.
Profile the group again to see how much of the step is now collective time.
Revert the degree alone and re-measure to confirm the layout was the cause.
Check whether the enlarged group now spans nodes instead of staying on the fast intra-node fabric.
Establish whether the added traffic is bandwidth bound, since tensor parallelism communicates inside the layer's critical path.

variants.hint: The most communication-heavy group belongs on the fastest link.
variants.explanation: Tensor parallelism puts communication inside the layer critical path, so a group that outgrows a fabric island pays for every microstep.

variants.title: Pick the parallel dimension
variants.context: Each parallelism dimension removes a different constraint. Data parallelism partitions the batch, sharded data parallelism partitions model state, tensor parallelism partitions a layer, pipeline parallelism partitions depth, context parallelism partitions long sequences, and expert parallelism distributes experts.
variants.prompt: One complete training replica fits comfortably on every device, but the team needs to process more examples per unit of time. Which dimension should be used first?
options: Data parallelism, replicating the model and synchronizing gradients across ranks.
Tensor parallelism, splitting each layer across a tightly connected group.
Pipeline parallelism, placing layer groups on separate stages.
optionFeedback: Correct: when a replica fits, partitioning the batch is the simplest strategy that removes the throughput constraint.
Splitting layers adds communication inside the critical path without solving a memory problem that does not exist.
Stages add bubbles and complexity to reduce per-stage state that already fits.
variants.hint: Start with the least complex strategy that fits the actual constraint.
variants.explanation: Complexity is added only for a measured memory or throughput constraint, so a fitting replica means the batch is the right thing to partition.

variants.title: Pick the parallel dimension
variants.context: Each parallelism dimension removes a different constraint. Data parallelism partitions the batch, sharded data parallelism partitions model state, tensor parallelism partitions a layer, pipeline parallelism partitions depth, context parallelism partitions long sequences, and expert parallelism distributes experts.
variants.prompt: A single layer's matrices are too large for one accelerator, and the devices in question share a high-bandwidth intra-node link. Which dimension fits?
options: Pipeline parallelism, so the oversized layer gets a stage of its own.
Sharded data parallelism, so optimizer state stops being replicated.
Tensor parallelism, splitting the layer's matrix operations across that group.
optionFeedback: A stage still has to execute the whole layer on one device, so the layer still will not fit.
Sharding persistent state does not make one oversized layer computable on a single device.
Correct: partitioning inside the layer is what makes an individual layer fit, and it belongs on the fastest link.
variants.hint: Ask what unit is too big: the batch, the persistent state, the layer, or the sequence.
variants.explanation: Tensor parallelism is the dimension that splits an individual layer, and its traffic sits in the critical path so it stays on the fastest link.

variants.title: Pick the parallel dimension
variants.context: Each parallelism dimension removes a different constraint. Data parallelism partitions the batch, sharded data parallelism partitions model state, tensor parallelism partitions a layer, pipeline parallelism partitions depth, context parallelism partitions long sequences, and expert parallelism distributes experts.
variants.prompt: Model state fits on each device, but activation memory blows up when the context length is raised to 128k tokens. Which dimension fits?
options: Sharded data parallelism, partitioning optimizer state and gradients.
Context parallelism, partitioning the long sequence across ranks.
Expert parallelism, distributing modules and routing tokens to their owners.
optionFeedback: Sharding persistent state does not reduce activations, which grow with context length.
Correct: activation memory that scales with sequence length is what context parallelism partitions.
Expert parallelism addresses mixture-of-experts modules, which is not what is growing here.
variants.hint: Identify which memory term is actually growing before choosing where to cut.
variants.explanation: Persistent model state and activation memory grow for different reasons, so a context-length problem is solved by partitioning the sequence.

variants.title: Read the collective
variants.context: The collective determines what each rank owns after the operation. All-reduce leaves the same reduced result everywhere, reduce-scatter leaves each rank its own reduced shard, all-gather reconstructs shards temporarily, and point-to-point sends move activations between neighboring pipeline stages.
variants.prompt: Match each communication primitive to what every rank owns once it completes.

pairs.label: All-reduce
pairs.detail: The same reduced result is present on every participating rank.

pairs.label: Reduce-scatter
pairs.detail: Each rank keeps only its assigned shard of the reduced values.

pairs.label: All-gather
pairs.detail: Shards are collected so participants can temporarily reconstruct full parameters.

pairs.label: Point-to-point send
pairs.detail: A neighboring stage receives activations or gradients directly.

variants.hint: Ask what each rank holds after the call, not what it sent.
variants.explanation: The primitive defines the ownership contract, which is why substituting one for another changes both correctness and memory.

variants.title: Read the collective
variants.context: The collective determines what each rank owns after the operation. All-reduce leaves the same reduced result everywhere, reduce-scatter leaves each rank its own reduced shard, all-gather reconstructs shards temporarily, and point-to-point sends move activations between neighboring pipeline stages.
variants.prompt: Match each training pattern to the primitive it relies on.

pairs.label: DDP synchronizing gradient buckets
pairs.detail: Every replica needs the identical averaged gradient.

pairs.label: Fully sharded training reducing gradients
pairs.detail: Each rank should end up with only its own gradient shard.

pairs.label: A module that needs its full parameters for one forward pass
pairs.detail: Shards are collected just long enough to compute.

pairs.label: Streaming micro-batches between two stages
pairs.detail: Tensors move directly to the neighboring stage.

variants.hint: The pattern tells you what state has to exist afterwards.
variants.explanation: Fully sharded training differs from DDP precisely in the primitive it uses for gradients, which is what keeps its persistent memory low.

variants.title: Read the collective
variants.context: The collective determines what each rank owns after the operation. All-reduce leaves the same reduced result everywhere, reduce-scatter leaves each rank its own reduced shard, all-gather reconstructs shards temporarily, and point-to-point sends move activations between neighboring pipeline stages.
variants.prompt: Match each observed symptom to the communication explanation it points at.

pairs.label: Many tiny collectives dominate the step
pairs.detail: Launch and network latency, not bandwidth, is the limit.

pairs.label: One rank skipped a collective and the job hangs
pairs.detail: Peers wait indefinitely rather than producing a partial answer.

pairs.label: Stages sit idle at the start and end of every step
pairs.detail: Too few micro-batches leave visible pipeline bubbles.

pairs.label: Layer-internal traffic crosses node boundaries
pairs.detail: A communication-heavy group was placed off the fast fabric.

variants.hint: Separate the symptom that is about bytes from the symptom that is about ordering.
variants.explanation: All ranks must call compatible collectives in the same order, and bandwidth problems and latency problems need opposite fixes.

variants.title: Size the job
variants.context: Topology is arithmetic before it is engineering. World size is the product of the parallel degrees, the persistent mixed-precision Adam state is 16 bytes per parameter before sharding, and each device keeps a reserve for activations and collective buffers on top of model state.
variants.prompt: A dense hybrid job uses data-parallel degree 8, tensor-parallel degree 4, pipeline-parallel degree 2, and context-parallel degree 1. How many ranks must be launched?
variants.hint: The degrees are a topology contract that has to match the launched ranks exactly.
variants.explanation: World size is the product of the parallel degrees, so 8 times 4 times 2 times 1 gives the number of ranks the launcher must provide.

mistakes.feedback: That adds the degrees; world size is their product.
That leaves out the pipeline-parallel degree, so a third of the layout has no ranks.

variants.title: Size the job
variants.context: Topology is arithmetic before it is engineering. World size is the product of the parallel degrees, the persistent mixed-precision Adam state is 16 bytes per parameter before sharding, and each device keeps a reserve for activations and collective buffers on top of model state.
variants.prompt: A 40 billion parameter model is trained with the 16 bytes per parameter mixed-precision Adam proxy, fully sharded across 64 data-parallel ranks on 8 nodes. How much persistent model state does each rank hold?
variants.hint: Full sharding divides the state across ranks, not across machines.
variants.explanation: The proxy gives 640 GB of persistent state for 40 billion parameters, and full sharding divides that across the 64 data-parallel ranks.

mistakes.feedback: That is the unsharded total; full sharding partitions it across ranks.
That divides by the 8 nodes rather than by the 64 data-parallel ranks.

variants.title: Size the job
variants.context: Topology is arithmetic before it is engineering. World size is the product of the parallel degrees, the persistent mixed-precision Adam state is 16 bytes per parameter before sharding, and each device keeps a reserve for activations and collective buffers on top of model state.
variants.prompt: Each accelerator exposes 80 GB, and the plan reserves 25 percent for activations and temporary collective buffers. How much is left for persistent model state per device?
variants.hint: The reserve is carved out before model state is allowed to claim anything.
variants.explanation: The reserve is subtracted from device memory first, and the remainder is the capacity a sharding strategy has to fit persistent state into.

mistakes.feedback: That is the reserve itself rather than what remains for model state.
That adds the reserve instead of subtracting it from device memory.
